newsitem.title: FRANCE: Winter barley harvest nearly complete in Champagne-Ardennes.
newsitem.headline: Winter barley harvest nearly complete in Champagne-Ardennes.

text.p: The winter barley harvest is nearly complete in the Champagne-Ardennes region in northeastern France and reports from the fields suggest the crop may fare much better than anticipated and yields could exceed last year's levels, crop analysts said on Wednesday.
The harvest was due to have started on July 1 but rain pushed back the starting date by about a week, forcing farmers to carry out combining operations at record speed.
"With the exception of the Haute-Marne and northern Ardennes areas, the winter barley harvest is almost over," said an official for the local ONIC grain office in Chalons-Sur-Marne.
Initial results show a wide variety in yields with some farmers reporting yields as high as 8.5 to 9.0 tonnes per hectare.
This led local crop officials to upgrade their yield estimates for the whole region to 7.3-7.4 tonnes for six-row winter barley and to 6.9-7.0 tonnes for two-row winter barley.
This would compare with 7.1 tonnes for six-row barley and 6.8 tonnes for two-row barley achieved last year.
"This is a good surprise, this is much better than expected," the official said.
Latest area estimates for winter barley are around 112,000 hectares, that is 2,000 hectares more than in 1996.
Prolonged drought in the spring had raised fears yields might be hit but the crops proved resilient. Wet weather in May and June was also beneficial.
The first barley cuts also eased fears that wet conditions in the last growing stage could hit quality.
"Contrary to expectations protein content did not rise and specific weight did not decline," the official said.
Barley needs a protein content of below 11 percent to qualify for malting.
The rain caused some unwanted germination in the fields though damages appear to be very limited.
The spring barley harvest will start within two weeks and yields are pegged around 6.5 tonnes against a revised 6.39 tonnes last year. About 109,000 hectares has been sown against 104,500 in 1996.
Average regional yields for soft wheat were forecast at around last year's levels of 8.2 tonnes per hectare.
High moisture levels in late June and early July led to disease outbreaks, particularly a mushroom disease that attacks the leaves and may threaten quality and yields.
But it was premature to say if this was a widespread problem, officials said.
"The yield potential for wheat is above last year's but we do not know yet how much damage was caused by the disease," one official said.
Analysts now say 423,000 hectares of soft wheat was planted in 1997 against 427,000 last year.
-- Dominique Vidalon, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
